children: Asian stock markets were subdued after U.S. markets were closed overnight for the Labor Day holiday, while the Japanese yen continued to strengthen against the dollar.

Regional markets on Tuesday lacked cues from New York, and investors are now awaiting the U.S. consumer-price index report due Friday. The inflation data are likely to solidify expectations about whether the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at its mid-September meeting.
U.S. consumer prices are expected to rise 0.4% on month in August, while prices excluding food and energy will likely increase 0.2%, according to consensus estimates.

"Equity markets are closely monitoring incoming macroeconomic indicators as the Federal Reserve's next policy meeting approaches," said Devarsh Vakil, head of Prime Research at HDFC Securities, in commentary. "Investors are carefully balancing signs of labor market resilience against cooling inflation pressures to forecast whether the central bank will implement further interest rate adjustments," Vakil added.

South Korea's Kospi rose 2.1%, Japan's Nikkei Stock Average edged 0.2% higher, and China's Shanghai Composite added 0.4%. Meanwhile, Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index fell 0.3%, Singapore's FTSE Straits Times Index declined 0.4%, and Taiwan's Taiex shed 0.3%.

In foreign-exchange markets, the Japanese yen continued to gain ground against the dollar, bolstered by expectations of faster interest-rate increases by the Bank of Japan and potential investment inflows into Japanese assets.

Expectations for a quicker pace of rate increases have mounted since last week, when BOJ policy board member Hajime Takata urged a flexible approach to tightening. He noted that the central bank's 2% inflation target had nearly been achieved and that the risk of prices overheating was rising.

The U.S. dollar was recently 0.5% lower at 153.53 yen after earlier touching Y152.87, its lowest intraday level since Feb. 17, according to LSEG data. The yen is now stronger than it was following the joint intervention by Japanese and U.S. authorities in July.
Meanwhile, crude-oil futures rose as traders parsed developments in the Middle East.
"Saudi Aramco's oil facilities in Jazan came under fresh attacks on Monday," ANZ Research analysts said, citing a media report.

"The recent escalation of the Middle East conflict has increased the likelihood of a prolonged standoff, punctuated by calibrated military action by the U.S. and Iran," the analysts said. "This could see Persian Gulf supply remain constrained through the rest of 2026," they added.
Front-month West Texas Intermediate crude oil futures rose 1.8% to $93.08 a barrel, and front-month Brent crude oil futures advanced 0.7% to $97.69 a barrel, according to ICE data.
